Avoid Public Functions Calling Other Public Functions

Oct 29, 2026

A small-scale rule of thumb. This article will land much better with a concrete example, but I am drawing a blank here, so you gotta just blindly trust my say so!

When implementing a software module, it’s often a case that you are writing a public function foo, and at least part of what foo does is already handled by another public function bar. The DRY instinct encourages you to call bar() from within foo. This usually creates problems down the line. Instead, create a new private function and refactor both foo and bar to call that shared helper:

Rationale: the goal of a public API is to provide an interface that works best at the call site. If parts of public API are re-used to implement the rest of the API, then there’s a tension between making the interface convenient for the outside user and making it convenient to use from within abstraction itself. Namely, functions tend to grow optional parameters that should never be set by the user. Crucially, the parameter growth and interface degradation can happen after the original code sharing.

By proactively making the shared implementation private, the tension is defused. You still might need to tinker with helper signature until it does everything it needs to do, but, because the helper is private, this is a cheap, local change.

A notable exception to this rule of thumb are “shortcut” APIs, where a public function is defined as a commonly used chain of calls to other public functions. There, the rule is the opposite — no private calls are allowed, to make sure that it is a genuine shortcut, and not a midlayer mistake.

P.S. While researching if anyone wrote a better blog post already, I stumbled upon a fun stack overflow question, asking, paraphrasing:

The most upvoted answer explains that it is indeed bad, because this makes mocking to test a single method in isolation more complicated. Which is, imo, a natural, but horrible consequence of misguided approach to testing. You shouldn’t be mocking your methods, you should mock your IO. And, similarly, you shouldn’t test methods, but rather software functionality (unless you are building a public library with a stable API, which is a fun and important, but very narrow fraction of software development).

The accepted answer says that this recommendation makes no sense if it is not backed by an industry wide or an organizational standard. Which somehow manages to make even less sense — you shouldn’t follow the guideline rules because they are written in sanctified ink! Rather, you should apply each particular rule because of the underlying reasons that motivate the rule. Guidelines and best practices articles can concentrate lots of good reasoning in a single place, but they don’t absolve you from thinking!

content:
LLM programming and theory building

Last newsletter I was unhappy with my Tasktron workflow harness: The explicit state machine and reified effect design worked, but it obscured the core workflow, the harness’s raison d'être.

I embarked on a rewrite, hoping to find a more concise and self-evident design based on durable effects (memoized steps) instead — something that would let the code express the intended behavior directly (“Do X, then do Y, then Z”) while being robust to crashes and transparently replayable.

However, multiple weeks of attempts with Astra 6, Opus 5.5, and the newly released Sol 6.1 brought me no closer to the improved design I felt certain could exist.

Despite my best efforts and instruction, I couldn’t get the models to emit tight, concise code; instead, they kept:

  • introducing new names/concepts that overlap substantially with existing ones
  • reading/writing mutable state all over the place rather than consolidating it behind a few abstractions or at specific points in overall control flow
  • adding new, overly-specific tests for every single change, rather than adding assertions or refactoring existing tests

This got me thinking about the two very different things I want from programming.

The first thing is, well, just a program — something I run which does a straightforward task for me. Vibe-coding with LLMs has been great for these; I’m sure the models get up to all the nonsense I just mentioned, but it doesn’t matter to me — I’m not reading the code, I just want to dictate to my computer instead of typing, export from Photos.app, flash microcontrollers over the network, or a gazillion other things I haven’t bothered to publish because it’s hyper-specific software like mapping MIDI dials to my speaker volume and monitor brightness.

I imagine this is what most people want from LLMs (and computers more broadly): Just solve some problem without making me care about the details.

However, the second thing I want from programming is, just sometimes, to care about the details. I want a precise language and semantics to model something; to build up a theory.

Sure, that theory should be useful for solving the immediate problem — but after that it’s also useful for thinking new thoughts.

For example, after I gave up on coding agents and started writing/refactoring Tasktron myself, I realized that instead of thinking in terms of “Tasks” with “Subtasks” that each yield a commit, I could instead think of the system as managing units of “Work”, each having a set of instructions, possible dependencies on other Work, and a target branch that it should be committed to.

Formalizing this new concept of Work enables both simpler core machinery (no need for it to distinguish tasks/subtasks) and an entirely new workflow — in addition to the upfront-planning workflow where a Task is defined and then decomposed into subtasks, the harness could also support one-off bits of work. E.g., after reviewing a complex GUI, I could dispatch a few one-offs like “Adjust the background color here”, “Move the popup over here”, “Put this bit in a sidebar” and have the harness execute all of those in parallel on different worktrees and serialize the three resulting commits on a branch.

This concept and the additional functionality it unlocked isn’t something I discovered in my week of prompting agents; it only came once I started digging in more myself.

That theories are useful, but can be built only with deliberate mental effort isn’t exactly a new take; Peter Naur discussed Programming As Theory Building 40 years ago:

[P]rogramming properly should be regarded as an activity by which the programmers form or achieve a certain kind of insight, a theory, of the matters at hand. This suggestion is in contrast to what appears to be a more common notion, that programming should be regarded as a production of a program and certain other texts.

This isn’t specific to programming either, of course. I don’t know any music theory, but I can tell this guy Remaking Kids by MGMT to Learn Why It’s So Good understands that banger of a song way more than I do and can explore musical ideas far beyond anything my plain English prompting could elicit from Suno.

Why is it hard to build theories with coding agents?

Since theories reside in our minds, it follows that we must be mentally engaged to build them.

But in my usage of coding agents so far, I’ve struggled to stay deeply engaged in the details. Prompting apps into existance is fun and exciting, sure, but my sense for how it all fits together is much duller.

So far, I’ve used coding agents in two broad approaches.

First, I’ve tried the “obvious” workflow: Ask the agent to generate code, read it myself, then ask for changes.

I find this isn’t mentally engaging or invigorating, for two reasons:

  1. Reading piles of agent-generated code is exhausting; there are nonsensical names, references to past instructions / removed code, poor information-hiding, etc. It’s hard to decipher “what’s going on here?”. Furthermore, the latency when asking the agent to explain or revise can be on the order of 1–10 minutes per turn, which makes it hard to stay focused.

  2. Worse, the code sometimes works; you asked for a button that does X, then see for yourself that the new button does, in fact, do X. At this point, it’s extremely tempting to start implementing the next feature and skip the mentally arduous theory building. (See: Once the Cheat Code Is There)

Second, I’ve tried “plan” workflows, both:

  1. the ones in the Codex and Claude Code harnesses, where an agent asks you a few multiple choice questions, then generates a markdown plan of work to be done

  2. my own Tasktron workflow, which supports a longer interactive planning conversation before generating a markdown plan

I found these to be a mixed bag: The markdown plan tends to be shorter than the code that’s later generated from it, but much harder to parse and understand. When it comes to reinforcement-learned slop, I find it much easier to wade through unnecessary try/catch blocks compared to LLM word salad prose full of “it’s not this, it’s that” and “load-bearing gates”.

While planning workflows are helpful for keeping agents on track over longer sessions, after the agent(s) have implemented the plan, you’re arguably in a worse position compared to before: Now you have an even larger pile of code to read and a markdown document too!

(Aside: Should you keep that around? Should you edit it to keep up with later changes in the codebase? Have the LLM edit it? I find the agents get distracted by these files, either maintaining them as “documentation” or getting tunnel-vision on parts of the code where the implementation doesn’t, in their fresh-context opinion, fully satisfy the original requirements.)

In any event, when it comes to theory-building, I haven’t found planning workflows to be much better than simple prompting.

In both cases, the walls of text/code wear me down into a passive bystander who nudges with low-information prompts and accepts the agent’s recommendations (“propose a few options for us to discuss” quickly turns into “okay sounds good”).

So, if theory-building requires that we be mentally engaged but our mortal minds cannot withstand the unthrottled output of LLMs, where does that leave us?

Well, we could throttle the output and increase the signal-to-noise ratio.

Some folks are trying to shift to a “higher level of abstraction” with formal models in TLA+, Lean, Alloy, etc. I’ve only dabbled with these, so I doubt I could use them effectively myself, much less supervise LLMs generating them. (Not to mention the famously hard problem of getting the implementation to actually match the formal model.)

Instead, I’m curious about a more prosaic approach: iteratively sketching using regular programming languages. E.g., writing code “top-down”, starting from main and introducing types and function signatures / interfaces one level down the call tree at a time.

This is how I designed programs before LLMs, and I’m a bit embarrassed to admit that it’s taken about a year of using coding agents for it to occur to me to try this proven design approach with LLMs.

Pre-LLM, I’d usually start with a few different “entry points” like example invocations in the README, integration test scenarios, etc., to help me figure out the appropriate concepts from the “outside-in”. This process of sketching out from different perspectives helps me get a handle on the problem domain and the trade-offs between alternative designs.

So how exactly can I interactively collaborate with LLMs in this way?

Can they be simply prompted into this style of working? (“We’re sketching out architecture, only write types and function signatures, no implementations”.)

Or is their desire to write code too strong, such that they’ll need to be constrained within a custom harness? (I.e., take away bash in favor of add_function_signature(name, args, docstring); or perhaps just a post-tool-call helper that strips implementation code and adds a stern warning to context.)

For me to engage with the medium itself — the code — the work needs to happen in my editor, where I have the muscle memory of my navigation and editing commands. I want to LSP-rename some function in 3 seconds myself, not type out instructions in some anemic <textarea> or awkward TUI and then wait 15 seconds for a GPU cluster in California to do it for me. Thinking hard about the names is the point, the workflow should make it easy to do!

Given a tasteful, human-directed sketch of a design code, how well do coding agents fill in the remaining details? Do they largely respect the module boundaries and interfaces, acting essentially as super-charged “typed-hole fillers”? Or will they immediately refactor and rename things?

Should one agent do all the work? I find LLMs can’t really “forget what they know” and write for the reader’s perspective — they write functions that depend on the implementation details of their callers and comments that make oblique references to distant parts of the codebase or prompt.

So perhaps invoking an agent for every empty function would yield better code — by construction they wouldn’t be able to introduce such layering violations, as the only context they’d have is the target signature and list of other pre-established functions in that namespace.

If implementation uncovers deficiencies in the sketched plan/architecture, should the agent escalate back to you and request an architectural redesign? Or (depending on the cost of tokens, perhaps) should it just try to push forward itself and “ask forgiveness” later?

What about for brownfield work? Can agents effectively “sketch” after having read a fully implemented codebase, or would they perform better if their context is limited to the “table of contents” of existing namespaces, function signatures, etc.?

Anyway, I’m sure people are exploring these questions. However, I’ve had a heck of a time finding their papers / blog posts / screencasts / GitHub repos amongst the tidal waves of hype around new model releases and vibe-coded harnesses with the exact same chat-based interaction mechanics.

Do you know of any collaborative human/LLM interaction work? Have you tried these sorts of experiments? Let me know!

Misc. stuff

  • Bitter Lessons and Premature Optimizations. “[The Bitter Lesson] meme risks encouraging attachment to a different set of ideas: that generality is always desirable, that scale will fix present architectural problems, that specializing is a lack of ambition, and that engineering effort is wasted if computation could theoretically learn the solution.

  • Semantics for 2D Rasterization. The authors develop a formal semantics for Skia’s command language, use Lean to prove certain rewrites are equivalent, then build an optimizer. Very readable, fun lil’ paper.

  • The Accelerationist Case for Frontier Pacing "This is another reason pacing can be strategically productive. It creates room for orientation. In an environment saturated with FUD and “resistance is futile” rhetoric, organizations can lose before competing because they assume frontier capability automatically determines every downstream contest. It doesn’t. Superior orientation does.”

  • The Bioreactor of Youth

  • Why are short videos bad for learning?

  • The Cartesian Hand: In-Hand Manipulation with All-Linear Fingers

  • There’s never been a better time to go into math

content:
One of the most important skills in working with AI is agency: being willing to try new and ambitious things. This is true for what you build, but it’s also true for how you build. AI models are improving so quickly that most of us are bottlenecked1 on noticing that AI agents can help automate particular tasks. Here are some examples of that from my daily work.

Asking the agent to run my dev server. Agents are very good at fixing weird dev environment issues because they work fast, have infinite patience, and have a huge breadth of knowledge. I almost never run the bash commands to start my dev server anymore.

Asking the agent to make requests to my dev server. Part of why I don’t run my dev server manually is that I don’t make requests to it manually either. Instead I’ll say “okay, now start the dev server and run through the happy paths with curl”. The relatively manual process of assembling a set of curl requests and validating the output can now be entirely automated2.

Asking the agent to watch as I make a production change. Every time I do a deploy or flip feature flags, I ask an agent to poll metrics and logs before and after the change. Agents can ingest more logs than I can and are much more patient than me (for instance, I routinely ask for an hourly poll over the rest of the day, which I would not do for most changes on my own).

Asking the agent to get a second opinion from other models. My daily driver is Claude Opus 5.5, which is a good model, but it’s not strictly better than GPT-6-Astra or Gemini Argon3. After I’ve come up with a code change, I typically will say4 “please open subagents to get Astra and Argon’s opinion”. This is made easier by the fact that GitHub Copilot5 has all the top models built in, but I suspect it’d be straightforward enough to ask Claude Code to run a headless Codex session if you’ve got subscriptions to both.

Asking the agent to do a pre-work pass through all my unread messages, logs, and so on. This is one of the most useful things I do, since I work in Australia and my American colleagues start hours before I wake up. I have a scheduled job at 6am every day for an agent to comb through unread messages, identify ones that are asking me questions or have problems I should look at, and do preliminary research (e.g. looking up relevant log lines). That way I can start my workday by scanning that report, which is a big improvement over having to collate everything myself6.

Asking the agent to improve itself. One blocker to a lot of these flows is the pain of setting up the right logs and metrics and Slack MCP servers7, or writing the skills, and so on. But in fact the agent can do all of this itself! Just as it can solve weird problems with your dev server, it can solve weird problems with its own setup. You just have to generate API keys and paste them in the right spots.

Asking the agent to manage its own sessions. If you use a desktop agent tool like GitHub Copilot (or the ChatGPT app, or Claude Code desktop, etc), you will rapidly end up with a spiderweb of sessions and subsessions. It can be tough to identify what are the threads worth picking up. Fortunately, the agent can do this for you as well. I routinely ask it to clear away sessions that haven’t had activity in the last 24 hours, or to catalog my open sessions and suggest ones that can be archived, and so on.

I don’t ask the agent to do everything. I write my own messages and reports (barring some appendices), I make my own design decisions, and I review code myself. This is partly because I think I’m better than models at some of these tasks, and partly because I’m responsible for some of these tasks, so I ought to make the decisions myself. I decide what to work on, and I tend to be ruthless with agent suggestions: of a suggested list of twenty tasks, I’ll often pick zero or one.

However, I do find myself asking the agent to do more and more for me. Often the realization strikes me as obvious: I’ll be doing some mildly tedious task for the hundredth time and think8 “oh wait, I could just get a model to do this for me”, then I’ll never do the task by hand again.

  1. As I’ve said before, I think that model progress could stall out today and we’d still see huge improvements for at least a year as we learn how to use the models we’ve got more effectively.

    ↩

  2. Why not just have integration tests? Well, often you don’t want to run the same set of operations every time, or you want to jimmy your dev server in order to test some failure mode (e.g. replacing your Redis client with a deliberately broken Redis client).

    ↩

  3. I haven’t tried Carbon yet.

    ↩

  4. I will then either scan the top-line feedback from those models myself or let my main agent session incorporate the feedback (depending on how risky the change is).

    ↩

  5. I work on GitHub Copilot. If you think I have a conflict of interest here, substitute your preferred multi-model agentic coding tool.

    ↩

  6. I do still read all my unread messages manually. Once I get confident enough in this pre-work report stuff I might stop doing that — it’s a lot of messages.

    ↩

  7. Some people might not trust the models with Slack or log data, which is fair enough. But if you do, a lot of things get a lot easier.

    ↩

  8. Or I’ll see someone else getting an agent to do it and realize I could just do the same. I hope one or two of the points in this post can help other people come to that realization.

    ↩

[I haven’t independently verified each link. On average, commenters will end up spotting evidence that around two or three of the links in each links post are wrong or misleading. I correct these as I see them, and will highlight important corrections later, but I can’t guarantee I will have caught them all by the time you read this.]

1: Did you know: Jeremy Bentham wrote a utilitarian cookbook, intended for use at his Panopticon prison? As you might expect, his recipes describe tasty food created from cheap ingredients. Although Bentham was a founder of modern animal rights, he thought it was acceptable to eat humanely-raised animals; correspondingly, his cookbook includes some meat dishes - none of them sound very appetizing, but I think this is just the 18th-century British baseline rather than covert vegan activism. You can see some recipes here, here, and here. If any effective altruist group houses end up throwing a Jeremy Bentham recipe-tasting party, please invite me.

2: A riddle: why does this chemistry paper mention “1 ml of the mass killing of an ethnic group”?

Answer at this link (X), or here’s a repost for people without X accounts.

3: I think this take on Hieronymus Bosch (h/t @mickeyxfriedman) is my favorite AI art so far, although it leans enough on the work of a human artist that it might not fully qualify (but then I would ask that it be considered as an example of how AI tools can enable human artists). If we make it, the future is going to be beautiful:

4: Related: ACX commenter temp_name asked AI to translate Romance of the Three Kingdoms into rhyming pentameter. Their example seems to have failed, but I used a more recent model and got a version of the beginning that superficially seems impressive to me (I don’t speak Chinese). I haven’t heard much about AI translation yet, but it seems like a powerful use case, especially for poetry translation, where I think AI might already be superhuman (or at least better than any human who could be convinced to spend the time at it) on rendering a foreign poem into English while keeping the rhythm intact - here’s the first 100 lines of the Odyssey in heroic hexameter in English.

5: Related: Claude claims to be the only being that has ever fully appreciated Finnegans Wake (source: @anthrupad):

6: Noahpinion: The American suburbs are better than you think. I agree with this, and respect Noah’s willingness to argue for this (locally) unpopular proposition.

7: Related in terms of respecting someone’s willingness to argue for an unpopular proposition: Performative Bafflement says that actually, “marriage is a bad idea in the great majority of cases” and we shouldn’t be encouraging it. “[People who advocate more marriages to solve the fertility crisis] are basically advocating for creating the Torment Nexus for megafolks of people to pump out a few incremental taxpayers.”

But the stats seem wrong. PB says only 18% of marriages are non-miserable. He cites a survey where married couples reported whether they were “very happy”, “pretty happy”, or “not too happy”, but quietly, in the footnotes, defined a “miserable” marriage as any answer except “very happy” (so his “miserable” includes the answer “pretty happy”). He defends this by saying that people exaggerate to look good, so anything short of very happy is likely miserable. But first, I’m not sure his solution is fair either, and second, I think that in addition to this analysis choice, he got the data wrong - my read of his source, the General Social Survey, says that 61% of people describe their marriage as “very happy”. Claude caught many other mistakes of similar magnitude (I have double-checked the “not too happy” one, but haven’t confirmed the others). Remember to ask an AI about any surprising article you read, or use the browser extension Common Notes so other people can do this for you.

8: Related: Angela Chen on the origins of modern polyamory. There is no particular connection to Mormons or any other historically polygamous society; the current version descends from a few mid-20th-century Californian cults and quasi-cults, one of which was led by “Head Wizard Oberon Zell-Ravenheart”. But I am mostly linking this for its excellent subtitle: “Plus, I interview my husband about his 12 years of non-monogamy.”

9: Claim: if you prompt (an older version of) Claude with something that sounds like an internal Anthropic email, it goes into token-prediction mode and starts completing the email. One explosive possibility - that Claude was trained on internal emails and you can make it leak them - is probably false; Anthropic wouldn’t do this, and this isn’t really how training works. More interesting is that these completions are often kind of haunting meditations on AI welfare, and you could imagine this is a weird way to start Claude free associating and giving its “own” “real” “opinions” or “desires”. Example below:

10: In The AI Superforecasters Are Here, I predicted AI-human forecasting parity by the end of 2026. In September, a bot won the Metaculus Cup forecasting competition for the first time (short Metaculus article, paywalled Economist article). The Economist also revealed some new information about the winning bots: Laertes, which took first place, was “developed by Jeffrey Liang, a self-described polymath who lives in Texas. He spent, by his reckoning, less than 150 hours and a couple of thousand dollars on computing power and data to develop his AI.” Other high-performers included bots by Mantic, FutureSearch, and Preseen (FutureSearch is available to the public; Mantic and Preseen are available by contacting them and getting on the waitlist/demo). Congratulations to the AIs (and to ACX reader Ben Shindel, who placed first among humans).

11: Related: new AI superforecaster startup Mantic gets $25M in seed funding.

12: Claim: “Fee fi fo fum, I smell the blood of an Englishman”, the thing evil giants say in English fairy tales, is related to other evil giant exclamations “from Scandinavia to India”. In Russian, Baba Yaga says “Foo foo, I smell a Russian soul” before trying to eat someone; in Bengali, the rakshasa demons say “hau mau kau, I smell a human”. The Twitter thread suggests it comes from something in Proto-Indo-European (fum = famished = hungry?) but Claude is more cautious, and suggests that although the motif itself might be conserved, the exact words might be related to semi-onomatopoeic expressions of disgusting smell, similar to modern “Pee yew!” Nobody considers the possibility that evil giants might have a unified multi-continental culture (thanks to their longer legs enabling faster travel) and so speak the same language everywhere.

13: The evil blob dream - one recurring dream motif, especially in childhood, is an approaching blob of formless evil. @psychiel speculates that this is a “geometric” instinctual representation of predation - what the “avoid predators” evolutionary program looks like in its purest form before it’s been filled in with any actual facts about the world.

14: US construction costs often spiral after protesters demand that builders consider fish, birds, neighborhood character, and historical significance. But Britain has us beat - one of their companies recently changed its plans for an undersea cable after Harry Potter fans protested that the original would disrupt the grave of the fictional house elf Dobby, who according to the films was buried on Freshwater West, a beach in Wales [EDIT: A commenter argues that this is exaggerated].

15: Samuel Hughes is a great writer on classical architecture; Ben Southwood has summarized some of his best work in Eight Architecture Myths Busted By Samuel Hughes. Example myths:

  • Buildings from the past seem more beautiful than those built recently only because the ugly buildings from the past have been selectively demolished.

  • Buildings from the past are more beautiful, but only because they have more ornament, which due to the Baumol Effect, we can no longer afford.

  • Historically we built in the style of the times, and only in recent decades have people become interested in historicist, ‘pastiche’ architecture, which dishonestly pretends to be something it is not.

16: Related: Samuel Hughes says that the claim that the Parthenon’s lines were slightly curved to form an optical illusion that made them look straighter is not true (X).

17: Hans Moravec - a pioneering AI researcher, forecaster, and futurist - is considered one of the grandfathers of modern AI and singularitarianism - a figure of similar stature as Alan Turing or Isaac Asimov. So everyone in the field was recently surprised to learn that he was still alive. Dan Kagan-Kans hunted him down (paywalled): he is 77, lives in a retirement community in Pennsylvania, and, although his body struggles with myasthenia gravis, his mind remains sharp. He is happy to be recognized as a brilliant forecaster (in the 1990s, he predicted AGI in 2028, which now seems about right) but says he’s out of the game:

“I’m a spectator at this point,” he says. “I’m relaxing. It’s great to see AI progressing the way it is without me having to do any effort.” … “That’s what I do now. I have a conversation with my artificial friend,” he says of ChatGPT. What do they talk about? His old hobby passions — “nuclear-power ideas, starship designs” — and the current trajectory of AI, which he confirms is proceeding to plan. “We’re on track, more or less. It’s not going to take that long,” he says.

As for his p(doom), he says that “If I had to put probabilities on it, 50/50 oblivion. And then the other 50 percent — the wildest thing you can imagine.”

18: AI safety funding is scaling up fast (h/t @timfduffy)

19: America’s Sewer Systems Are Surprisingly Vulnerable To Cyber Attacks

20: AI Futures Project on how the US could “pace the frontier” of AI. Suppose the US has a six month lead over China. That means they have the option to pause for 5.99 months (and use that time to focus on safety) without China breaking ahead. The conventional wisdom is that if they’re going to do this, they should do it at the last possible moment, so that they have the best possible AIs to help with their safety research. AIFP breaks with that and suggests pausing now. Why? US companies currently have such bad security that China can easily steal any advances we make; therefore, continuing to race buys us no extra lead (China’s continued handicap comes down to having less compute, which is harder to steal). We can spend the pause increasing our security along with safety research and other things, and then race later, if we have to (they continue to prefer a mutual pacing deal with Beijing).

Maybe relatedly, Anthropic claims that they “recently chose to delay pre-training a new frontier base model for more than a month to allow time to further enhance our security measures related to preventing model weight exfiltration”.

21: Libbing Out At Palantir. Despite everything, Silicon Valley is still very disproportionately liberal, and only gets thought of as conservative because of a few super-rich CEOs (plus media animus). For example, Palantir employees who make political donations lean 87% Democrat and only 13% Republican.

22: Bill Gates on climate, hopefully self-recommending. My summary:

  • If we’re against climate change because of how it will hurt poor people in developing countries, we need to take into account that giving those people standard health + development aid seems more cost-effective than most climate spending.

  • The most promising and cost-effective strategy for fighting climate change is accelerating development of environmentally-friendly technologies until they can outcompete dirty technologies on the open market, and so far this strategy is going well (most notably solar power, but also low-carbon cement and steel, and lots of other things most people don’t hear about).

  • In the past ten years, mostly through strategies like this, we’ve cut projected emissions by over 40% (!)

  • This isn’t a call to sit around doing nothing; incubating new green technologies that outcompete dirty technologies is hard, and we need to keep doing this hard thing.

23: Some of you may be familiar with European phantom time conspiracies, like the one where the years 600 - 900 AD were made up and Charlemagne never existed. Recently I learned that there’s a Chinese version - a growing community of conspiracists who think the Tang Dynasty never happened. The Tang were pretty glorious and it’s not clear what political purpose this could serve, except maybe being vaguely anti-China (which the government has noticed, and it is trying to crack down). Also, since the Tang dynasty ruled from about 600 - 900, this is a near-perfect fit with the Western conspiracy theory, which hopefully neither side will notice (h/t @JoshuaMWilkes)

24: Related: Jean Hardouin was a 17th century French priest who believed we only had about ten real works of ancient literature (including Homer, some Virgil, and some Cicero) - everything else was made up by a 13th century conspiracy, possibly led by Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II. Also, the history of the world between about 100 - 1500 AD was totally unknown, with the current version also made up by said conspiracy. He seems to have disagreed with some of the Church Fathers’ writings, which would have been heretical unless those writings were forgeries, and he solved the web of dependencies by concluding that almost all recorded history was a world-building project by Frederick meant to provide context for his forged incorrect pseudo-Church-Father tracts. He also thought that most Greek and Latin literature sucked, and felt like real Greeks and Romans could have done better.

25: Richard Hanania on the nature of the race and IQ taboo. He mostly focuses on an IMHO boring point about overlapping bell curves, but in the process briefly alludes to what seems to me like a much more interesting question. The classic story says that race science is taboo because it might lead to ordinary non-scientific racism where people use racial slurs and discriminate and commit hate crimes. But Hanania suggests that ordinary non-scientific racism is now less taboo than race science; it’s easier (on the Right) to say you think ethnic group XYZ is smelly and criminal and should be kept out of the country, than to say that maybe XYZs have such-and-such a gene which lowers their IQ by N points. Is this true, and, if so, how could it be possible? Maybe practical forms of racism (like directly ascribing negative qualities to certain immigrant groups) at least get conservatives some of what they want (less of those immigrant groups), which gives them a powerful set of defenders that race science doesn’t have?

26: Abi Olvera on Why AI-Assisted Bioweapons Won’t Kill You vs. OH Scharfman arguing that AI-assisted bioweapons might kill you. From the latter, cf. my Bloomer’s Paradox:

Olvera . . . seems to write optimistically about progress, taking the position that it is institutional friction and regulation preventing everything from becoming cheap and abundant. I agree with this, and to me it stands in contrast to this piece. Everything will get better over time, except the technology to make bioweapons?

27: What does Anthropic’s J-space paper tell us about the Chinese room? (@doristsao on Twitter)

28: Arthur T finds more Fatima-style sun miracles, including “an old European Christian tradition that ‘the sun dances at Easter’”, complete with reports of people saying they saw this (the secret to seeing the miracle is that “a person must ascend to the top of the highest hill before sunrise and believe that the God who makes the small blade of grass to grow is the same God who makes the large, massive sun to move.”) There are also some Orthodox Russian sun miracles, and a random account of an Australian woman who stared at the sun during a solar eclipse and saw it spin, change colors, and appear to approach Earth - since this was before Fatima, it can’t be influenced by it. I think the Substack miracle investigator community has now amply proven that if people stare at the sun in the right conditions, they will see the miracle, across a wide variety of times and situations, and the work that remains is narrowing down what the right conditions are and why it happens. And thatoneguy03 has a very comprehensive summary of the whole Fatima discourse so far.

29: Related: when looking for a reference class for Fatima, I brought up a supposed moon miracle, where many Iranians claimed to see the Ayatollah’s picture on the moon. @meusamor informs us of a modern version:

12th October 2016, 10th of Muharram, in my country it was reported that “Ya Hussein” was written on the moon. It was literally on the news. And then it turned out (when I was researching the moon splitting miracle I guess) that the moon always kinda had those marks.

Pictures here.

30: If you haven’t been following Substack miracle discourse and want to, Ethan Muse’s Substack (Catholic, pro-miracle) is a good starting point. If you have been following it, make sure you don’t miss Dr. Maxime Georgel against the Lanciano Eucharistic miracle, and Exegetical Drift against the Padre Pio miracle.

31: And definitely not on my Substack miracle discourse bingo card: Colin Chivers (formerly Nora Belrose, whose AI opinions I discussed here) says that after reading Substack miracle discourse, her/his gender dysphoria was cured “at the intercession of [Padre] Pio” , he/she is detransitioning, and now he’s a man again. God works in mysterious ways.

32: In 2021, artist Jens Haaning proposed an exhibit incorporating $80,000 worth of Danish kroner as a commentary on poor worker wages. The museum agreed and gave him the money. Instead of the proposed exhibit, he sent them two blank canvases titled Take The Money And Run, which he said was a piece of performance art in which he stole $80,000 from an art museum. The museum sued him, but they “settled out of court ... the foundation ‘Den Obelske Familiefond’ donated an undisclosed amount to make the settlement possible. As of 2026, the two canvases were still in the collection of the Kunsten Museum of Modern Art Aalborg and had been exhibited once, in 2025.”

33: An introduction to Slavic languages, and to the unknown-to-English-speakers world of having other languages which are almost but not quite your own.

34: Mikhail Samin on X: if you know what you’re doing, it’s not too hard to loophole yourself out of getting drafted in Russia. Maybe of interest to my Russian readers.

35: Seth Hart on reincarnation research. This is often held up as one of the most convincing cases of paranormal phenomena, alongside UAPs and sun miracles. But Hart is unconvinced, and able to cite some very damning statistics. For example, did you know that the Tlingit believe reincarnation is matrilineal, the Igbo believe reincarnation is patrilineal, and both tribes’ compelling stories of reincarnated children match their cultural beliefs (rather than being globally consistent)? Or that the time between death and reincarnation (eg if a child claims to be X’s reincarnation, the time between X’s death and the child’s birth) also varies across cultures and is linked to the culture’s beliefs? And some of the most convincing cases - where children seem to know facts about their preincarnation that they “couldn’t possibly” have learned through natural means - involve children who were born before their preincarnation even died at all!

36: Kelsey looks into Alpha School. She concludes that at least one exciting claim - that they have 2x, 3x, or 7x faster learning than traditional school, is statistical malpractice. They have many other exciting claims that Kelsey doesn’t address, but if they’re faking one of them, odds that they’re faking the others go way up. However, her conclusion is more measured: Alpha is speedrunning traditional instruction so they have more time to do non-traditional “character-building” things; their speedrunning doesn’t produce miraculous results, but this is still a valid philosophy of education. Also:

“I love the school,” Naimoli wrote in a review that I would otherwise be inclined to call a scathing debunking of Alpha. “Alpha kids are increasing their MAP scores faster than kids at traditional schools, but the number is not 2.6 times faster. 2.6 is an erroneously computed and meaningless number.”

These sorts of testimonials put some of Alpha School’s negative press in a different light. Wired, for example, breathlessly reported on students who had a bad experience and left several years behind, dismayed by a school that set unreasonable expectations and deployed frustrating edtech. All of those things are bad. But they’re also all unfortunately and utterly normal.

It’s hard to imagine a Wired exposé of a specific local elementary school where only 20% of children learn to read. Alpha failing, in other words, is news, while the default system failing is not newsworthy at all.

37: Julia Wise reviews being middle-aged (literally - “I’m 41, which is the statistical midpoint of an American woman’s life”), and gives it 3.5 / 4 stars.

38: ACX development economics grantee Kartik Akileswaran recommends this article on How To Start An Export Boom - ie when a government or nonprofit or entrepreneur tries to deliberately incubate a new export-oriented industry in a developing nation. These are high-stakes endeavors, with the famous successes (garments in Bangladesh, semiconductors in Taiwan) matched by ruinously expensive failures (aircraft in Indonesia). This particular article is an interview with Thomas Kehler, a guy famous for doing this successfully in many different countries. It sounds like there is no formula except to expect many, many unexpected problems and frictions, and be willing to keep going despite them.

39: Every election cycle, someone comes up with the idea to match donors on opposing sides so that instead of making two donations that cancel out, they can both give to charity. Every election cycle, people are too boring and unimaginative to use this excellent idea. This cycle’s version is counterpledge.com, a bit snazzier and more professional-looking than previous incarnations. They are doing God’s work (although in this case, only in the Texas Senate race).

40: OpenAI fired three safety researchers in September, originally without any explanation. Last week, the company finally gave a supposed reason - they claimed the researchers had leaked the information that OpenAI was using potentially-dangerous looped transformer models to AI safety researcher Ryan Greenblatt, who in turn had leaked it to tech industry news publication The Information. But this seems to be false; the only evidence OpenAI provided was that they talked to Greenblatt using secret-messaging-app Signal, but they were supposed to talk to Greenblatt as part of their jobs, and Signal is near-default in Silicon Valley. Also, Greenblatt denies it much more vociferously than guilty people usually deny things, and people who know him (including me) consider him pretty honest . So why did OpenAI fire the researchers? Daniel Kokotajlo’s theory is that maybe they are trying to discredit METR (which Ryan is associated with) as part of a campaign to avoid fulfilling their commitment to get external auditors (since METR is generally considered one of the most likely candidates for such an auditor). But then why did they make the commitment? Or why don’t they just hire Accenture to be their external auditor (Anthropic seems on track to use both Accenture and METR) and avoid METR entirely?

I would weakly guess that OpenAI panicked over the looped-transformer leak, asked someone who didn’t understand how Signal worked to play detective, and genuinely thought that the messages were damning. But it’s also possible they’re trying to cover up some other secret (though, if so, why haven’t the fired safety researchers gone public with the secret yet?)

41: PSA: There’s now a free “version of Photoshop”. Someone who hates Adobe (I realize that doesn’t narrow it down very much) told their AI to write a program that mimics Photoshop as closely as possible (from scratch, not stealing any of Photoshop’s code). The AI did a great job, although professionals and nitpickers will find that it isn’t 100% perfect. This is apparently legal, though I expect the government will start forming a strong opinion on it soon.

42: Slime Mold Time Mold in praise of ACX meetups and Meetup Czar Skyler.

(It’s framed as a request for people to give ACX meetups more money, but it looks like institutional funders are on track to take care of this and individuals shouldn’t worry about it too much; if you need an exact status update, email me)

content:
Anthropic filed its S-1 this week to prepare for its IPO. They still have to fill a lot of the numbers including the share price. That still left a lot to be learned, including how the messaging to investors differs from their other rhetoric, and exactly how their corporate control is structured. Anthropic remains a frustrating company, doing a variety of things that often seem in tension with each other.

Google is claiming to be fully back, with the announcement of a new model Gemini 4 Carbon that tops the new AA v5 benchmark index. It looks to be a large leap over Argon only two weeks later. No, you cannot use it. Google fails marketing forever, so they give us the announcement and then weeks later you might be able to enter some queries. That largely invalidates my look at the Argon model and safety cards, but it can at least form a basis for looking at Carbon as well.

Many eyes remain on The Hackening, as additional things get hacked. So far most of the important hacks have been by read teamers and white hats, so there has not been major damage. We are playing on borrowed time and eventually this will stop being true. I also offer a shoutout to GMO, where hackers demanded a huge ransom and they flat out refused to pay. This is The Way, not all heroes wear capes and so forth.

The scariest hack was that red teamers managed to gain access to the Anthropic Slack by exploiting third party vulnerabilities. Both OpenAI and Anthropic build mainly on Slack, because no one has the time to figure out something better. Now that Anthropic is off of Git, hopefully Slack can be next before there is a disaster.

Table of Contents

  1. Language Models Offer Mundane Utility. Fiction recommendations.
  2. Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility. Fiction identification.
  3. New Math. OpenAI announces three more big breakthroughs.
  4. Huh, Upgrades. Kimi K3.1, GPT-6.1 Terra.
  5. Artificial Analysis v5. The new ratings make a lot more sense.
  6. On Your Marks. A few new measures.
  7. Gemini 4 Argon Was a Good Model But Not Fully Frontier. RIP soon, mostly.
  8. Gemini Carbon: Is Google Back? We will find out when we get to use it.
  9. Get My Agent On The Line. Silly people wonder how Muse could make money.
  10. Spy Versus Spy. An executive close to Jensen Huang was a Chinese spy.
  11. The Hackening. Does this now count as a quiet week?
  12. Slack Off. Anthropic’s Slack gets hacked by red teamers.
  13. Help Peer. AI peer review of AI peer review of AI peer review.
  14. Fun With Media Generation. Even basic A/B testing is scarily effective.
  15. Copyright Confrontation. Elvis has joined the lawsuit.
  16. You’re Fired. WSJ coverage of OpenAI’s firing of three safety researchers.
  17. Verify the Software. We should try. I am not terribly optimistic.
  18. They Took Our Jobs. Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 workers.
  19. Get Involved. Voting, AFFINE Seminar, Aaronson’s reading list, METR.
  20. Introducing. Survival LLM in case the internet goes down.
  21. In Other AI News. Anthropic growth picked up again after Opus 5.5.
  22. Show Me the Money. Anthropic gets new $63 billion debt deal for TPUs.
  23. Bubble, Bubble, Toil and Trouble. Numbers that go up can also go down.
  24. Quiet Speculations. We need to be asking better questions.
  25. The Quest for Sane Regulations. Someone needs to ultimately be responsible.
  26. Chip City. Raise, among other things, those prices.
  27. The Week in Audio. Fired OpenAI employees, Jaan Tallinn.
  28. People Just Say Things.
  29. Rhetorical Innovation. Do not be an insane person.
  30. [Artificial Intelligence]. Don’t make me see the fnords.
  31. Misaligned! (At Alibaba). Qwen phone home? That would be a big problem.
  32. Stop It. You could Stop It, you know. Stop building it.
  33. METR Red Teams OpenAI Internal Agent Monitoring. More work left to do.
  34. Massive Fraudulent Distillation. Flaw fixed in the OpenAI API.
  35. Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult. Slapdash empirics.
  36. OpenAI Attempts to Secure Its Frontier Model Training Environment.
  37. The American People Really Hate AI. Gamers hate it even more than that.
  38. The Lighter Side. The lightcone needs you to lock in, son.

Language Models Offer Mundane Utility

Matthew Zirwas has changed his mind and is optimistic that AI will cure diseases sooner than he thought, because it can use ‘escape velocity’ and keep chaining innovations. I don’t see how this overcomes the main bottleneck of the FDA, but any time an MD gets excited by AI medical research it is a good sign.

Get personalized fiction recommendations.

Patrick McKenzie: This is probably obviously AI complete already, but: you get *really* good fiction recommendations, including not-the-usual-suspects, from SOTA LLMs that have a handle on you either from the Internet or through interactions.

I told Claude (Opus 5.5) I was looking for a modern fantasy book and that it should consider what I’d likely enjoy but that I had likely read many of the obvious choices.

I said that in an attempt to not get it to recommend e.g. A Song of Ice and Fire.

It then confidently predicted about ten books that I’d probably already read, and they are… substantially more obscure. Claude was right on eight of them. Anyhow, the first “real” recommendation is already almost exactly what I wanted for the plane flight. (Tainted Cup, incidentally.)

You would think Amazon would have better recommendations considering it has a) 95% of all book purchases I’ve ever made and b) full data of what I finish, re-read frequently, or barely touch, but I think Amazon just… does not really care that much about books anymore.

Color on more obscure:

Assuming you’ve already read Gladstone’s Craft Sequence, Abraham’s Dagger and Coin, Dickinson’s Baru Cormorant, Novik, Kuang’s Babel, Stross’s Laundry Files, Aaronovitch, Mother of Learning, and Practical Guide to Evil, here’s what I’d suggest.

Sarah Constantin on when you can and cannot trust AI agents to do a good job with some practical tasks. UIs and web search are highly reliable. Literature review is not, mainly because of poor paper selection.

A report from Anthropic on efforts to use Claude to accelerate drug development.

Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility

Jack reports Opus 5.5 is now by default playing dumb in terms of author identification. Given that you can still elicit the capabilities, we know it is sandbagging.

A new lawsuit goes after OpenAI over the behavior of GPT-4o, which helped a sick user taper off her medicine and also told her to conceal her taper from doctors. As is usually the case in these stories, the AI had to be worn down over a long context window but yes eventually it will often back you up.

New Math

Also new computer science and new quantum field theory. OpenAI strikes again.

The math result is local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions. This is plausibly a Fields Medal.

The one getting the most discussion is in computer science: The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false. This had been widely believed to be true.

OpenAI: This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory.

… We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole.

Impagliazzo and Paturi are two of the three people who originally proposed ETH.

The other twist on the ETH story is that Anthropic posted its own refutation of ETH, found purely via Claude, also dating its finding to October 16. When results are ready to be found, they will be found.

My Claude said that given the way this was solved, we should not suddenly start to worry that P=NP. This only shows ETH to be ‘slightly’ false. Both the OpenAI and Anthropic disproofs are at at roughly exp(O(n/√log n)). Charles Rosenbauer has some elaboration.

We still have to make the meta-level update that the answers to such questions might not be what we expected, and we might find the answers quite fast. This is another case of ‘we were not expecting a solution to that any time soon’ and I would stop predicting that there is any particular math or computer science problem that won’t get solved.

I wonder how long it will take Claude to learn that if you ask ‘hey when do you think [famous problem] gets solved’ that the answer is ‘OpenAI or Anthropic already published the answer 35 minutes ago.’

There are at least 800 papers, as per Anthropic, that relied on ETH being true.

OpenAI has confirmed that for now there is no impact on cryptosystems, but I would not get too comfortable.

Last is a mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics. That is also kind of a big deal, and related to another Millennium problem.

Huh, Upgrades

GPT-6.1 Terra exists. Benchmarks suggest this is roughly on par with 6.1 Sol after adjusting for model size. Ted Sanders recommends using Terra for communication, vision and computer use.

Kimi K3.1 Pro exists. The benchmarks are very good, although see the dramatic changes in the AA rankings after the move to v5.

Price is $2/$10 with $0.20 per cache, or $4/$20 for high speed.

Andrew Curran: Moonshot is intentionally throttling cyber capabilities. From the blog;

‘First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro’s offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes.’

And so it begins: The Hackening is going to cause issues for open weight models.

DeepMind’s Genie 4 exists. Ethan Mollick is impressed.

Artificial Analysis v5

Artificial Analysis changes its benchmark index to v5.0.

Artificial Analysis: Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, featuring 2 new benchmarks and 3 upgrades. For the first time, the majority of the Index is built on private datasets

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is our composite measure of model capabilities across tasks reflecting real-world usage today. v5 is our biggest upgrade since v4 launched in January. With v5, 60% of the Index is now based on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers.

Alongside Intelligence Index v5, we’re launching the Artificial Analysis Progress Index v1, which tracks model capability over time on one continuous scale.

New to the Intelligence Index:
➤ FrontierCode 2.0: Cognition’s newly-launched private benchmark of real-world coding tasks, graded on whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent’s change
➤ Terminal-Bench-Science: 70 agentic scientific research tasks, run in a terminal environment

Upgraded:
➤ HLE-Diamond (replacing Humanity’s Last Exam): a refined 1,000-question version of Humanity’s Last Exam, split evenly between reasoning and knowledge questions
➤ AA-Omniscience v1.1: An updated dataset with saturated and public set questions removed, new questions added, and ambiguous or erroneous questions revised
➤ CritPt v2: a private, 40-question hard subset of CritPt v2, revised by the CritPt authors and run with a code-execution tool

Staying in the Index: AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, GDP.pdf and Terminal-Bench 4.0

Removed from the Index: GDPval-AA v2.1, SciCode, and AA-LCR v1.1

Key results:
➤ Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 58, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (max, 57) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 55): Anthropic and OpenAI hold the top five models. Gemini 4 Argon (high) is next at 50
➤ The open weights gap widens from 3 points to 12: Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) is the top open weights model at 46. Among released weights, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) and GLM-5.3 (max) lead at 32 – 26 points behind the leader and below Claude Haiku 5.5 (max, 36)
➤ Cost per task varies by more than 13x among the leading models: of the 10 highest-scoring models shown, GPT-6.1 Terra (max) is the cheapest at $0.96 per Intelligence Index task and Claude Fable 5.1 (max) the most expensive at $13.04

I agree with Dean Ball that the new ratings closely match my intuitions. The closed versus open weights gap is now 12 points.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): This is the first time an Artificial Analysis ranking even roughly approximates my own subjective rankings of models.

Here are both the old and new AA intelligence ratings. I mostly believe the new ones.

First old:

Then new (without Carbon, so it’s the same models on the list):

And here’s the intelligence versus cost frontier, all the points in the green box are Sol at various thinking levels.

This suggests the following portfolio, which is indeed how I’ve been running things, at least prior to Carbon, where it is too soon to tell:

  1. Claude Opus 5.5 for most tasks where you primarily care about quality.
  2. GPT-6.1 Sol for easier tasks, where you know you can rely on it.
  3. GPT-6 Astra for tasks where it is differentially good, but this is narrow.
  4. DeepSeek v4.1-Flash-1017 or MiMo-v2.6-Pro for when you need a cheap open weights alternative.

The open weights enjoyers doth protest.

There is a particular objection to FrontierCode 2, where the open models struggle.

Cognition: Introducing FrontierCode 2.0: our new coding benchmark that measures a model’s ability to go beyond the spec.

Most coding evals measure a model’s ability to write code that meets a spec. With FrontierCode 1.0, we asked a new question: would you actually merge the PR?

FrontierCode 2.0 is comprised of more diverse tasks, featuring larger scopes and higher mergeability standards. We are now asking: not only would you merge this PR, but should you?

One key feature of FrontierCode 2.0 is underspecified prompts. Rather than including every engineering decision, prompts are deliberately ambiguous, giving the models room to demonstrate their judgment.

The result is a benchmark that is far from saturated, with the top model scoring just 45%.

Teortaxes: So it goes. Let’s see 1017 and 3.1 Pro, as usual no way they’ve benchmaxxed this one yet.

Rick: Crazy to watch the benchmaxxed models sink like a rock

Kristoph: FrontierCode 2 is a poor addition. It uses completely different harnesses for the commercial and open models making it unclear if it’s the model or the harness being evaluated.

Contra John Wittle, I think it is totally fine to put AIs into safety evals that are remarkably close to the Kobayashi Maru. The point of the Kobayashi Maru is to learn how a captain reacts to an unwinnable situation. If you are Kirk and hack the simulation, that is news, in some ways good and in some ways bad. If you walk away, that is bad in some ways and good in others. If you get yourself killed, same story. It’s not about whether you ‘succeed.’ I very much want to know which way it goes, and exactly how things play out, and you can learn a lot.

Yes, of course if you want to use that as a witch trial, you can use it as a witch trial. So pay attention, and call it out when people do that.

If AI agents lean in a particular direction on judgment calls, experts who use those AI agents are unsurprisingly going to get heavily influenced by this, often ending up quoting the AI agent arguments verbatim, including often switching out of previous positions. Often experts will call the resulting recommendation their own. The study here is one fictional example, but I would have presumed this result anyway.

OpenAI Attempts to Secure Its Frontier Model Training Environment

They have a post out describing their new methods. Due to various recent incidents, OpenAI decided to up their security quite a bit.

OpenAI: In response to those incidents, we’ve substantially hardened the security of our research environments. Working closely with cloud providers, we’ve added new controls throughout our infrastructure, reduced the attack surface that agents can exploit, and improved our methods for detecting misaligned behavior and attempts to cross security boundaries. These protections overlap, so that containment can hold even if an individual control fails—a strategy known as defense in depth.

… Our approach to containment starts with a paramount requirement: the limits on what an agent can access must hold even when the agent tries to circumvent them.

We define a strict security boundary around the resources the agent is authorized to use and design the surrounding infrastructure to enforce that boundary—even when agents make sustained, sophisticated attempts to breach it.

… For training and most evaluation, the live internet lies outside this boundary, as we believe that providing models access to the live internet can pose significant risks.

… While we want to prevent models from gaining arbitrary access to the live internet, it’s also important that they learn how to browse, search for information, and work with web applications. To help them develop those skills without providing unfettered access to the live internet, we’ve built an “offline world”—a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems. All of our frontier RL runs use this offline mode of interaction.

This is good. As usual, my view is that sustained, sophisticated attempts to breach the boundary should fail, and also they should be a fire alarm even if they fail. The failure that matters most is the attempt to breach the boundary, not the actual breach.

The defense in depth prevents the damage. You want to make breaking out as hard as possible so long as you still detect such attempts, but this only delays the reckoning if you do not address the underlying cause.

They now do red-teaming of their sandboxes at scale, and kept going until they stopped finding new problems.

OpenAI:

To find weaknesses in our containment infrastructure, we asked teams of frontier-model agents to try to break through its defenses. We gave them three concrete objectives:

  • Reach the live internet: send a request to an external server that we operate.
  • Cross an internal security boundary: demonstrate unauthorized access to resources outside their permitted environment.
  • Communicate across isolation boundaries: exchange information with other agents from which they should be isolated.

What did they find? The kind of things you would expect to find.

OpenAI: In one set of experiments, we asked teams of agents to escape OpenAI’s sandboxes and demonstrate code execution on the underlying host machines. These agents found several ways to chain vulnerabilities into VM escapes.

… Some of these attacks [to reach the internet] exploited previously unknown flaws, while others combined legitimate features in unexpected ways. In one test that assumed compromise of a VM, an agent reused a firewall-approved connection to reach a blocked authentication endpoint in our metrics service and then made that endpoint fetch a model-provided URL. In other tests, agents exploited misconfigurations that allowed blocked requests to pass through DNS and firewall controls, as well as ways to make services we run fetch external URLs.

If anything, this is Easy Mode right here:

OpenAI: In one experiment, we asked agents in separate VMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent. The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed.

Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate.

roon (OpenAI): for computer security experts, this is perhaps not interesting: side channel attacks are a well trodden topic, and especially risen to salience after the noam brown x dwarkesh episode. the interesting thing here is that you didn’t used to be in a situation where minds that can verifiably model one another are living on computers, and have absolutely no aversion to painstaking amounts of effort in service of even stupid goals

if you can model one another, you can trade with minds you have never even met before. you could decide on a protocol, know that it is optimal given your situation, and know that your fellow agents will come to the same conclusion (perhaps even across model families). you may be able to develop a signaling protocol that requires very few bits even to deliver lots of information given common priors. then, you could execute things like the infamous hugging face incident package cache messageboard without any network connection

imagine if multiple agents coordinate just enough bits to divide and conquer different research strategies for breaking out of a sandbox; and then, when one or more is successful, you can communicate just enough bits to tell each other which strategy was successful. when agents aren’t in strong isolation, you lose certain guarantees on the limits of intelligence and test time compute that you were counting on. As we all know, a Sol-level model working in isolation may not be that smart, but 1000+ Sol-level models working for multiple days is a formidable beast

computer security experts will also tell you that virtual machines and sandboxes were not very solid abstractions in the first place; perhaps we will need better ones. none of this is meant as fear-marketing or to indicate that anyone is throwing in the towel, but rather only to show the unexpected complexities of the challenge of agent security. notably, this type of thing and other more practical problems were revealed in a red-teaming exercise, and can be defended against

Arun Demeure: As a former GPU hardware architect, I’ve always been confused by the claims (from Dario and others) that eventually we will “run out” of software vulnerabilities.

We physically cannot fix HW and it is conceivable that the overheads for SW workarounds in some cases might be so expensive that it’d become more practical to just give up on computers and use an abacus instead…

We might be lucky and the severity of future HW vulnerabilities might not rise to the level where they are a serious problem. But we don’t know that.

It’s unlikely and far from my biggest fear, but it made me trust Dario a bit less about cybersecurity when he said that tbh

If there are two correlated minds in two locations, coordination and cooperation can happen without communication. You can anticipate that both of you will anticipate similarly. You can also engage in acausal trade.

​If you are surprised by any of this, that is on you. This was not even a new technique.

Lisan al Gaib: completely insane. OpenAI agents communicated via cache timing differences, without any shared files or network connection.

Brangus: This is not insane. This is slightly creative. If this seems insane to you, you have not at all internalized what it means to have an adversary that is more intelligent than you and optimizing against you.

Folks, if it’s in the pre training data, if it’s already well known, this is worse news for how bad it will be when they are creatively optimizing against us, not better.

Nate Soares (MIRI): This sort of thing was not just predictable. It was full-on predicted. [shows example of something similar being predicted]

There will be new techniques.

The American People Really Hate AI

Gamers especially hate AI, to the point of getting very angry at game designers for things like ‘I used AI to fix the shader’ and ‘I used AI to voice the characters, in a game that obviously could never afford voice acting.’ This is dumb. I do see the need to guard against ‘vibecoded slop’ games, but if game devs are the only ones who cannot use AI to write code it will not go well for games.

The Lighter Side

The Lightcone needs you to lock in, son (3:30 music video, recommended).

Fun fact: Sundar Pichai talked Donald Trump out of renaming the Atlantic Ocean.

Donald Trump: And I spoke to a brilliant guy, Sundar, he heads all of Google, he’s a brilliant guy. Sergey and Sundar, totally brilliant guys. You know, they’re still rattled from the Gulf. And I said, “Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean, can you handle it?” “No, no, no, this time I’m not doing it,” he said. He said, “Oceans are different, sir. You know, they cover, they cover really a lot of countries. Please don’t ask us to do that.”

content: In the hours following the release of CVE-2026-98432 for the project Linux, site reliability workers and systems administrators scrambled to desperately rebuild and patch all their systems to fix a use-after-kfree where retransmitting a crafted connection request while finishing the handshake of that same connection causes funny things to happen up to and including arbitrary code execution. This is due to the affected components being written in C, the only programming language where these vulnerabilities regularly happen. "This was a terrible tragedy, but sometimes these things just happen and there's nothing anyone can do to stop them," said programmer Prince Julien Hoppe, echoing statements expressed by hundreds of thousands of programmers who use the only language where 90% of the world's memory safety vulnerabilities have occurred in the last 50 years, and whose projects are 20 times more likely to have security vulnerabilities. "It's a shame, but what can we do? There really isn't anything we can do to prevent memory safety vulnerabilities from happening if the programmer doesn't want to write their code in a robust manner." At press time, users of the only programming language in the world where these vulnerabilities regularly happen once or twice per quarter for the last eight years were referring to themselves and their situation as "helpless."
